# Part II. Web Scraping

Question 1: Scrape a table.

To begin I am uploading the libraries required for scraping a table from Wikipedia. I'll be using rvest for the webscraping, tidyverse for data cleaning and transformations, janitor to clean up the column names, and stringr for string manipulation. The link to the wikitable was saved into an `html` object.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(rvest)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(stringr)

html <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_of_Chicago")
```


```{r}
ca_table <- html |> 
  html_element("table.wikitable") |> #extracting first table from wikipedia page
  html_table() |> 
  clean_names() |> #keep names in lowercase
  select(no, name, population) #keep relevant columns


ca_table <- ca_table[-c(1, 79), ] #remove the rows with repeated info and the citywide totals

ca_table$name <- ca_table$name |> 
  str_remove("\\[\\d+\\]") #removing the brackets from the names list

ca_table$population <- ca_table$population |> 
  str_remove_all(",") #remove commas from the population row then covert to numeric

ca_table$population <- as.numeric(ca_table$population)

nrow(ca_table)
head(ca_table)
```

Then here I am filtering for the single row of West Town and the communities with the highest populations.
```{r}
ca_table |> 
  filter(no == 24)

ca_table |>
  slice_max(order_by = population, n = 5)
```

Question 2: Scrape with CSS selectors. 

```{r}
html2 <- read_html("https://books.toscrape.com/") #read the url for scraping and save into object

section <- html2 |> 
  html_elements("li.col-xs-6.col-sm-4.col-md-3.col-lg-3") 
#save the repeating section that contains the info

title <- section |> 
  html_element("h3") |> #extracting the title
  html_text2()

price <-  section |> 
  html_element("p.price_color") |> #extracting each book price
  html_text2()

availability <- section |> 
  html_element("p.instock.availability") |> #extracting the availability
  html_text2()

books <- tibble( #creating a tibble from the previous objects
  title,
  price,
  availability
)

nrow(books)
head(books)

write.csv(books, "books.csv") #saving the table into the documents folder
```


# Part III. Open Data API

```{r}
library(httr) # send requests (GET(), POST())
library(jsonlite) # parse JSON into data frames/lists

#saving the link from the city of chicago data portal
url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json"

#establishing the parameters to include the variables and values we are interested in
#saving them in an object
params <- list(
  'community_area' = 24,
  '$limit' = 1000,
  '$where' = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'", 
  '$order' = "created_date DESC",
  '$select' = "community_area, status, sr_type, created_date, closed_date"
)

#fetchning a response from the API using GET() function
res <- GET(url, query = params)

#converting the object into a dataframe and flattening in case of nested data frames
dat <- fromJSON(content(res, "text"), flatten = TRUE)

nrow(dat)
names(dat)
```
4. Interpret. [2 points] In 2 to 3 sentences, say what this summary suggests about service needs in 
West Town and name one thing the data cannot tell you. 
```{r}
dat |> 
  group_by(sr_type) |> 
  summarise(total_requests = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(total_requests)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The most common complaints in West Town have to do with graffiti, which are a nuisance if you are a shop owner, and an overall desire to have orderly and clean streets. Parking code enforcements, potholes, sign repairs, fused street lights, abandoned vehicles, and tree obstructions all make it dangerous especially when you are driving in the area. This dataset, however, doesn't tell us where exactly the complaint can be found or who made it.


BONUS
```{r}
library(lubridate) #for date/time conversion functions

dat |> 
  filter(status == "Completed") |> #filtering by complete and then converting UNIX timestamp to date object
  mutate(days_between = as_date(as_datetime(closed_date)) - as_date(as_datetime(created_date))) |> 
  group_by(sr_type) |> #grouping by complaint and then calculating the median
  summarise(median_days = round(median(days_between))) |> 
  arrange(desc(median_days)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

# Part IV. Census API

Step 1: Identify the variables. 
• Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income, “Total”: B25070_001E 
• Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income, "50.0 percent or more": B25070_010E
• Median Household Income: B19013_001

Step 2: Retrieve the data.
```{r}

library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)

acs <- load_variables(2024, "acs5")

rent <- get_acs(
  geography = "county", #getting the acs data by county level for 2024 5-year estimates
  variables = c(rent_total = "B25070_001",
                rent_half = "B25070_010", 
                hh_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024,
  state = "Ohio"
  )
```

Step 3: Clean and transform.
```{r}
rent <- rent |>
  select(-moe) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = "variable", #pivoting the data so that each variable has one column and 
              values_from = "estimate") |> #each county is on one row
  mutate(severe_burden_rate = (rent_half / rent_total) * 100) |>  #creating burden rate variable
  arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))

head(rent)

rent <- rent |> 
  separate(NAME, into = c("county", "state"), sep = "\\,") #bonus question, separating the column name

head(rent)
```

Step 4: Analyze.
```{r}
rent |> #computing the mean and median severe burden rate across counties
  mutate(median_sbr = round(median(severe_burden_rate)),
         mean_sbr = round(mean(severe_burden_rate))) |> 
  head()

#making the county variable into a factor and ordering them by the burden rate for both the 
#lowest and highest values
library(forcats) # load the library for ordering variables
rent_max <- rent |> 
  mutate(county = fct_reorder(county, severe_burden_rate)) |> 
  slice_max(severe_burden_rate, n = 5) |> 
  head()    #counties with the highest rates

rent_min <- rent |> 
  mutate(county = fct_reorder(county, desc(severe_burden_rate))) |> 
  slice_min(severe_burden_rate, n = 5)#counties with the lowest rates
```

Step 5: Visualize. [5 points] 
```{r}
library(ggplot2)

rent |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hh_income, y = severe_burden_rate)) +
  geom_point() + # Scatterplot of median household income against severe_burden_rate 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkgreen") + #adding a regression line with standard error
  xlab("Median Household Income") +
  ylab("Severely Burdened Household Rates") +
  labs(title = "Median household incomes per Ohio county and the rate of renters who are severely burdened") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#Bar chart of the top 5 and bottom 5 counties in Ohio. Using factor reordered data
rent_max |> 
  ggplot(aes(county, severe_burden_rate)) + 
   geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#f68060", alpha=.6, width=.4) +
    coord_flip() +
    xlab("") +
    ylab("Severe Burden Rate for Renters") +
    labs(title = "Ohio counties with the highest rate of burdened renters") +
    theme_bw()

rent_min |> 
   ggplot(aes(county, severe_burden_rate)) + 
   geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#f68060", alpha=.6, width=.4) +
    coord_flip() +
    xlab("") +
    ylab("Severe Burden Rate for Renters") +
    labs(title = "Ohio counties with the lowest rate of burdened renters") +
    theme_bw()
```

Step 6: Reflect. [4 points] 

1. What relationship do you see between income and severe rent burden in Ohio, and what might 
explain it?
There seems to be an inverse relationship between the amount of household income in Ohio with the rate of burdened renters. The rent must be high in places with comparably low wages, where individuals are forced to then use most of their income on rent. Those who are severely burdened also seem to be in the majority of the counties.

2. What are two limitations of using county-level ACS estimates to decide where to target rental 
assistance?
The county level is too large of a geographical area to make targeted policy changes. It would be more useful to use zip codes or block levels to narrow down the specific groups of people who need rental assistance. Narrowing down the scope of the area can also help in identifying a potential cause for the high rates of burden.
